items.question: When is a credit agreement treated as reckless under the National Credit Act?
items.reference_answer: It is reckless if the credit provider failed to carry out the required affordability assessment, or carried it out but still concluded the agreement even though the information showed the consumer did not understand the risks, costs or obligations or would become over-indebted.

evidence.quote: the credit provider failed to conduct an assessment as required by section 81 (2), irrespective of what the outcome of such an assessment might have concluded at the time

items.answer:
A credit agreement is treated as reckless when a court or Tribunal declares it reckless in proceedings in which the agreement is being considered, as determined under the relevant Part of the National Credit Act. [nca_act_34_2005, p.55]

During a debt-review assessment, reasonable grounds to suspect that an agreement is reckless require the debt counsellor to report it to the National Credit Regulator or the Magistrate’s Court, depending on the recommendation made. [nca_act_34_2005, p.55]

items.question: Who must a debt counsellor tell when they suspect an agreement under review was granted recklessly?
items.reference_answer: The debt counsellor must report the suspected reckless credit agreement to the National Credit Regulator, or to the Magistrate's Court where the counsellor recommends a court order.

items.answer:
If the debt counsellor rejects the debt-review application or recommends voluntary debt rearrangement, they must report the suspected reckless credit agreement to the National Credit Regulator. [nca_act_34_2005, p.55]

If the debt counsellor recommends that the Magistrate’s Court declare the agreement reckless, they must report it to the Magistrate’s Court. [nca_act_34_2005, p.55]

items.question: What complaints-handling framework must a bank maintain for its customers under the banking conduct standard?
items.reference_answer: A bank must establish, maintain and operate an adequate and effective complaints management framework that ensures the fair treatment of complainants.

evidence.quote: A bank must establish, maintain and operate an adequate and effective complaints management framework

items.answer:
A bank must establish, maintain and operate an adequate and effective complaints-management framework that ensures the fair treatment of complainants and is proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of its business and risks, as well as appropriate to its business model, financial products, financial services and financial customers. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.15]

The framework must provide for relevant objectives and principles, allocated responsibilities, appropriate performance and remuneration standards, documented procedures for managing and categorising complaints, expected timeframes, escalation and review processes, record-keeping, monitoring, analysis and reporting to the governing body, and appropriate communication with complainants and their authorised representatives. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.16]

The governing body is responsible for effective complaints management and must approve and oversee implementation of the complaints-management framework, although that oversight may be delegated to a person with appropriate seniority and expertise. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.17]

Persons responsible for complaint decisions or recommendations must be adequately trained, have appropriate complaints-handling knowledge and skills, and not be subject to a conflict of interest. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.17]

The bank must categorise and record reportable complaints, maintain an appropriate internal escalation and review process, analyse complaint information on an ongoing basis to identify and manage conduct risks and prevent recurrences, and maintain transparent, visible and accessible complaint processes without charging complainants. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.18] [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.20]

Communications with retail complainants must use plain language. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.20]

items.question: What must banks do to check their operational resilience against international principles?
items.reference_answer: Banks must assess the adequacy and robustness of their current policies, processes and practices against the BCBS principles for operational resilience.

evidence.quote: Banks must assess the adequacy and robustness of their current policies, processes and practices against the principles for operational resilience issued by the BCBS

items.answer:
Banks must assess the adequacy and robustness of their current policies, processes and practices against the BCBS principles for operational resilience. [sarb_d10_2021_operational_resilience, p.3]

They must apply risk-based operational resilience controls aligned with their risk appetite and the nature, size and complexity of their operations. [sarb_d10_2021_operational_resilience, p.3]

They must address all BCBS principles through internal resources or outsourcing and third-party agreements without undue delay. [sarb_d10_2021_operational_resilience, p.3]

They must integrate the principles into their enterprise-wide risk management framework and apply them on a consolidated basis. [sarb_d4_2023_operational_resilience, p.1] [sarb_d4_2023_operational_resilience, p.2]

have in place an enterprise - wide and systematic approach to operational resilience in order to adapt to the changing environment and to sustain core business services. In March 2021 the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued a paper on principles for operational resilience.1 The principles aim to strengthen banks' ability to withstand operational risk-related events that could cause significant operational failures or wide-scale disruptions in financial markets. The principles contained in the BCBS paper must not be considered in isolation, but rather be integrated into a bank’s enterprise-wide risk management framework. The Prudential Authority (PA) published Directive 10 of 2021 on 14 December 2021. Based on developments in the local and international regulatory environment as well as the need for alignment on implementation timelines with other jurisdictions, the PA decided to extend the previously determined date for compliance. This directive serves to direct banks to consider the adequacy and robustness of the banks’ current policies, processes and practices related to operational resilience, against the best practices contained in the BCBS paper on principles for operational resilience. 1.

items.question: What must a registered debt counsellor do when their business address or contact details change?

evidence.quote: The Debt Counsellor must notify the National Credit Regulator immediately upon any change in contact details

contexts.text: 1 1. BACKGROUND Section 71(4) of the National Credit Act (“the NCA”) requires a debt counsellor, within (7) seven days of issuing a clearance certificate, to file a certified copy thereof with all credit bureaus. items.question: What is the statutory objective of the prudential regulator for financial institutions in South Africa?
items.reference_answer: To promote and enhance the safety and soundness of financial institutions and market infrastructures, protect financial customers against institutional failure, and assist in maintaining financial stability.

evidence.quote: promote and enhance the safety and soundness of financial institutions that provide financial products and securities services

items.answer: The statutory objective of the Prudential Authority is to promote and enhance the safety and soundness of financial institutions that provide financial products and securities services, promote and enhance the safety and soundness of market infrastructures, protect financial customers against the risk that those financial institutions may fail to meet their obligations, and assist in maintaining financial stability. [fsr_act_9_2017, p.66]

[fsr_act_9_2017, p.66]

items.question: What general standard of conduct must providers of over-the-counter derivatives meet?
items.reference_answer: A provider must at all times act honestly, fairly, with due skill, care and diligence, and in the interests of clients and counterparties.

evidence.quote: A provider must – (a) at all times act honestly, fairly, with due skill, care and diligence, and in the interests of clients and counterparties

items.answer: Providers must act honestly, fairly, with due skill, care and diligence, in the interests of clients, counterparties and the integrity of financial markets; communicate clearly, fairly and without misleading information; manage conflicts of interest fairly; observe proper market-conduct standards; comply with applicable laws, rules and regulations; and engage openly and cooperatively with the Authority, including disclosing material non-compliance and operational failures. [fsca_conduct_standard_otc_derivatives_2018, p.2-3]

BACKGROUND Section 71(4) of the National Credit Act (“the NCA”) requires a debt counsellor, within (7) seven days of issuing a clearance certificate, to file a certified copy thereof with all credit bureaus. Such filing must be accompanied by letters issued by the relevant credit providers providing confirmation that such accounts have been paid up or have become uncollectable the by operation of law. To enhance security of consumers’ data, compliance with the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (“POPIA”), and standardising processes, the National Credit Regulator (“the NCR”) has designated the Credit Bureau Association (“the CBA”) to provide and maintain an authentication platform to be used by debt counsellors for the filing of the certified clearance certificates and supporting documents. Debt counsellors have already been onboarded and trained on this authentication platform through various guidelines, circulars and training webinars conducted by the NCR.

contexts.text: , the basel committee on banking supervision ( bcbs ) has issued various new or revised frameworks or requirements during recent years for implementation by member jurisdictions. In this regard, on 7 December 2017, the BCBS issued the revised standardised approach (STA) and internal ratings-based (IRB) approach for credit risk. In September 2022 the PA issued proposed amendments to the Regulations relating to Banks (Regulations) to incorporate the respective requirements specified in the revised STA and IRB approaches for credit risk issued by the BCBS into the Regulations. The PA subsequently issued Guidance 3 of 2023 setting out the implementation dates of the outstanding regulatory reforms in South Africa. This directive must be implemented in accordance with provisions of the finalised Regulations, as and when amended. Any reference to Regulations must be interpreted as a reference to the finalised Regulations. Among other matters, the revisions to the STA and IRB approaches include new and adjusted threshold amounts used in the classification of credit risk exposures, the calculation of the minimum required capital and reserve funds, and regulatory reporting.

In March 2021 the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued a paper on principles for operational resilience.1 The principles aim to strengthen banks' ability to withstand operational risk-related events that could cause significant operational failures or wide-scale disruptions in financial markets. The principles contained in the BCBS paper must not be considered in isolation, but rather be integrated into a bank’s enterprise-wide risk management framework. The Prudential Authority (PA) published Directive 10 of 2021 on 14 December 2021. Based on developments in the local and international regulatory environment as well as the need for alignment on implementation timelines with other jurisdictions, the PA decided to extend the previously determined date for compliance. This directive serves to direct banks to consider the adequacy and robustness of the banks’ current policies, processes and practices related to operational resilience, against the best practices contained in the BCBS paper on principles for operational resilience. 1.

contexts.text: ( ias ) 39 was based on an incurred loss approach, ifrs 9 does not require a loss event to occur before a provision is raised. The expected credit loss (ECL) model required by IFRS 9, which takes into account forward-looking information, resulted in a significant increase in impairments raised by banks thereby affecting the available capital. The capital impact was managed through transitional arrangements. This Directive directs banks and auditors of banks regarding the classification of impairments as either general or specific under IFRS 9 post the conclusion of the transition period and replaces Directive 5/2017 issued in November 2017 1. Introduction 1.1 In July 2014, the IASB issued IFRS 9, which became effective for reporting periods commencing on or after 1 January 2018, replacing IAS 39, Financial Instruments: Classification and Measurement. 1.2 IFRS 9 fundamentally changed the way banks calculated provisions for credit losses/impairments given that IAS 39 impairments were based on an incurred loss model which required a loss event to occur prior to a provision being raised. Under

ifrs 9, it was important for regulatory purposes to define which provisions should be regarded as specific provisions ( sp ) and general provisions ( gp ). Given that a distinction between GP and SP did not exist under the accounting frameworks, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) recommended that regulatory authorities provide guidance to banks on how they should classify ECL provisions as either GP or SP, to ensure the consistency of categorisation by banks within their jurisdictions. 1.6 The Prudential Authority (PA), through its Directive 5/2017, provided clarity to banks conducting business in South Africa on how to classify ECL provisions as GP or SP. Further, the directive clarified the phase-in period of the day-one impact on common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital, calculated once at the point of transition, and other consequential adjustments. 1.7 The transitional arrangements were implemented to allow banks who elected such to rebuild capital resources following the initial negative impact arising from the introduction of IFRS 9 through increased impairments. These arrangements were in place for three years.

items.question: What must a credit provider assess before granting credit, and how recent must the affordability information be at approval?
items.reference_answer: It must take reasonable steps to assess the consumer's understanding of the risks and costs, repayment history, and existing financial means, prospects and obligations. The affordability check must be done within seven business days before initial approval or a limit increase, and within fourteen business days for mortgages.

evidence.quote: A credit provider must not enter into a credit agreement without first taking reasonable steps to assess
within seven(7)business days immediately prior to the initial approval of credit or the increasing of an existing credit limit

items.answer:
Before entering into a credit agreement, a credit provider must assess the consumer’s understanding of the proposed credit’s risks, costs, rights and obligations; debt-repayment history; existing financial means, prospects and obligations; and, where applicable, whether a commercial purpose has a reasonable prospect of success. [nca_act_34_2005, p.54]

The affordability assessment must calculate discretionary income and consider all monthly credit-agreement debt repayments, maintenance obligations and other necessary expenses. [nca_affordability_regs_2015, p.16]

The consumer’s debt-repayment history must be checked within seven business days immediately before initial credit approval or an increase in an existing credit limit, or within fourteen business days for a mortgage. [nca_affordability_regs_2015, p.16]

Where applicable, affordability documentation includes the latest three months’ bank statements, and variable monthly gross income must be averaged over at least the preceding three pay periods. [nca_affordability_regs_2015, p.14]

items.question: How fast must a debt counsellor issue a clearance certificate, and how fast must it then reach the credit bureaus?
items.reference_answer: The certificate must be issued within seven days after the consumer meets the re-arrangement obligations, and a certified copy must be filed with all credit bureaus within seven days of issue.

items.question: What must a credit provider report when it makes or amends a credit agreement, and why did the regulator single out consumers under debt review?
items.reference_answer: It must report the prescribed information to the national register or a credit bureau. The regulator found providers were not submitting payment profile information for consumers under debt review, leaving them with thin credit files.

evidence.quote: the credit provider must report either directly to the national register established in terms of this section, or to a credit bureau
some credit providers do not submit payment profile information of consumers who are under debt review to credit bureaus as required by the Act

items.answer:
When entering into or amending a credit agreement, other than a pawn transaction or incidental credit agreement, the credit provider must report the prescribed information, in the prescribed manner and form and within the prescribed time, either directly to the national register or to a credit bureau. [ncr_guideline_june_2025_credit_info, p.2]

The regulator singled out consumers under debt review because consumers who completed the process and received clearance certificates had no payment-profile information recorded on their credit-bureau reports, making new credit applications difficult and causing credit providers to treat them as thin-file consumers. [ncr_guideline_june_2025_credit_info, p.2]

In March 2021 the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued a paper on principles for operational resilience.1 The principles aim to strengthen banks' ability to withstand operational risk-related events that could cause significant operational failures or wide-scale disruptions in financial markets. The principles contained in the BCBS paper must not be considered in isolation, but rather be integrated into a bank’s enterprise-wide risk management framework. The Prudential Authority (PA) published Directive 10 of 2021 on 14 December 2021. Based on developments in the local and international regulatory environment as well as the need for alignment on implementation timelines with other jurisdictions, the PA decided to extend the previously determined date for compliance. This directive serves to direct banks to consider the adequacy and robustness of the banks’ current policies, processes and practices related to operational resilience, against the best practices contained in the BCBS paper on principles for operational resilience. 1.

items.question: What complaint-handling duties apply to banks and to credit providers, and how quickly must a credit provider act on a complaint referred by an ombud?
items.reference_answer: A bank must maintain an adequate and effective complaints management framework. A credit provider must attempt to resolve an ombud-referred complaint within fourteen business days.

evidence.quote: A bank must establish, maintain and operate an adequate and effective complaints management framework
The credit provider must attempt to resolve the complaint within fourteen (14) business days after receiving notification of the complaint from the ombud

items.answer:
A bank must acknowledge a complaint within a reasonable time, promptly explain the handling process, identify the responsible contact or department, provide indicative timelines, and explain internal escalation, review, and relevant ombud processes. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.20]

A bank must keep the complainant adequately informed about progress, delays and revised timelines, and the bank’s decision. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.20]

A bank must maintain processes for engaging relevant ombuds, communicate ombud availability and contact details at relevant stages, maintain records and analyse ombud-referred complaints, monitor ombud determinations and guidance, and comply with prescribed complaints-reporting requirements. [fsca_cs3_2020_banks, p.21]

Where an affordability-assessment complaint is referred by an ombud, the credit provider must attempt to resolve it within 14 business days after receiving the ombud’s notification. [nca_affordability_regs_2015, p.17]

Where the credit provider is a financial institution, an allegation of a reckless credit agreement may be referred only to the ombud with jurisdiction over that provider and must be procedurally resolved as a complaint under the Financial Sector Regulation Act. [nca_act_34_2005, p.88]

items.question: When must lifetime expected credit losses be recognised under IFRS 9, and how does the banking regulator want the resulting impairments classified?
items.reference_answer: Lifetime expected credit losses are recognised when credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition. The regulator directs banks to classify the impairments as either general or specific.

evidence.quote: measure the loss allowance for a financial instrument at an amount equal to the lifetime expected credit losses if the credit risk on that financial instrument has increased significantly
This Directive directs banks and auditors of banks regarding the classification of impairments as either general or specific under IFRS 9

items.answer:
Lifetime expected credit losses must be recognised when there has been a significant increase in the likelihood or risk of default since initial recognition, generally before the financial asset becomes credit-impaired or an actual default occurs. [ifrs9_project_summary_2014, p.20-21]

The Prudential Authority directs banks and their auditors to classify IFRS 9 impairments as either general provisions or specific provisions after the transition period. [sarb_d3_2023_accounting_provisions_ifrs9, p.1]

items.question: At what shareholding must a bank list a shareholder in its returns, and above what level did the original banking statute require permission to acquire shares?
items.reference_answer: Shareholders holding 1 per cent or more must be listed with their details. Under the 1990 statute, acquiring more than 10 per cent needed the Registrar's written permission, up to a ceiling of 17,5 per cent.

Currently section 70 of the Banks Act provides that, in the calculation of the aggregate amount of capital that a bank is required to maintain: (a) The sum of a bank’s primary share capital and primary unimpaired reserve funds shall be calculated by deducting from the amount thereof such amounts as may be prescribed. (b) The sum of a bank’s secondary capital and secondary unimpaired reserve funds shall becalculated by deducting from the amount thereof such amounts as may be prescribed; and (ii) taken into account to an amount not exceeding the sum of the bank’s allocated and qualifying primary share capital and allocated and qualifying primary unimpaired reserve funds. The aforementioned requirements of section 70 of the Banks Act imply that banks’ qualifying secondary capital and reserve funds may not exceed qualifying primary share capital and reserve funds, that is, the split may be 50:50. This process includes the maintenance of effective risk management and capital management by the bank.

have in place an enterprise - wide and systematic approach to operational resilience in order to adapt to the changing environment and to sustain core business services. In March 2021 the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued a paper on principles for operational resilience.1 The principles aim to strengthen banks' ability to withstand operational risk-related events that could cause significant operational failures or wide-scale disruptions in financial markets. The principles contained in the BCBS paper must not be considered in isolation, but rather be integrated into a bank’s enterprise-wide risk management framework. The Prudential Authority (PA) published Directive 10 of 2021 on 14 December 2021. Based on developments in the local and international regulatory environment as well as the need for alignment on implementation timelines with other jurisdictions, the PA decided to extend the previously determined date for compliance. This directive serves to direct banks to consider the adequacy and robustness of the banks’ current policies, processes and practices related to operational resilience, against the best practices contained in the BCBS paper on principles for operational resilience. 1.

items.question: Does Banks Act Circular 19/2004 still set the 10 per cent minimum capital-adequacy ratio that banks must hold?
items.reference_answer: No. Circular 19/2004 is not among the circulars confirmed as effective in Circular C1/2026, so it is deemed withdrawn; it recorded the 10 per cent ratio set in 2001.

contexts.text: the minimum required capitaladequacy ratio of 10 per cent has to consist of primary share capital and reserve funds will be reduced to 60 per cent. Consequently, the provisions of the press release of the Basel Committee in respect of innovative instruments, which press release limits the innovative instruments to 15 per cent of primary capital, are accommodated by amending the previously required ratio of 75:25 to 60:40, instead of the definition of primary share capital being expanded to include hybrid debt instruments. The above means that at least 60 per cent of the minimum required capitaladequacy ratio of 10 per cent has to consist of primary share capital and primary reserve funds without any reliance being placed on hybrid debt instruments. Since innovative instruments will not form part of the definition of primary share capital, a limitation with regard to hybrid debt instruments will not be imposed upon banks. contexts.section: 12. Further information on this Office’s policy decision on the qualifying
contexts.text: 12 This Office is of the opinion that the above-mentioned decision to adjust the minimum requirement relating to primary capital and reserve funds to 60 per cent of the minimum required capital-adequacy ratio and to address hybrid debt instruments separately(a) Is a better outcome than maintenance of the previously determined ratio of 75 per cent of the minimum required capital-adequacy ratio of 10 per cent to consist of primary share capital and reserve funds and amendment of the definition of primary share capital to include hybrid debt instruments subject to a limitation of 15 per cent of the primary capital and reserve funds in respect of the innovative instruments. (b) Means that banks are in a position similar to or better than they would have been had this Office maintained the previously determined position of 75:25 and had this Office allowed hybrid debt instruments to be included in the 75 per cent limit subject to a maximum of 15 per cent of primary capital and reserve funds. (c) Is prudent and eliminates unnecessary complexity from a regulatory, tax and accounting perspective with regard to the split between equity instruments and debt (liability) instruments. (d) Sufficiently accommodates international developments with innovative instruments.

contexts.section: 12. Further information on this Office’s policy decision on the qualifying
contexts.text: capital of a bank Based on the above information, the following decisions have been made: (a) Instead oftainting the definition of primary share capital; or (ii) diluting the primary capital base of a bank, with the inclusion of hybrid debt instruments in the definition of primary share capital, the previously determined ratio of 75:25 in respect of primary and secondary capital and reserve funds will be amended to give recognition to the fact that a hybrid debt instrument is a better form of capital than subordinated term debt, but a weaker form of capital than equity instruments. (b) To amend the provisions ofsection 70 of the Banks Act; (ii) regulation 21(6A) of the Regulations; and (iii) regulation 21(7) of the Regulations. The requirement that at least 75 per cent of the minimum required capitaladequacy ratio of 10 per cent has to consist of primary share capital and reserve funds will be reduced to 60 per cent.
